items.GOVERN 1.4: The risk management process and its outcomes are established through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on organizational risk priorities.
items.GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
items.GOVERN 6.1: Policies and procedures are in place that address AI risks associated with third-party entities, including risks of infringement of a third party's intellectual property or other rights.
items.MAP 4.1: Approaches for mapping AI technology and legal risks of its components, including the use of third-party data or software, are in place, followed, and documented, as are risks of infringement of a third-party's intellectual property or other rights.
items.MAP 4.2: Internal risk controls for components of the AI system including third-party AI technologies are identified and documented.
items.MEASURE 2.7: AI system security and resilience, as identified in the MAP function, are evaluated and documented.
items.MEASURE 2.10: Privacy risk of the AI system, as identified in the MAP function, is examined and documented.
items.MANAGE 2.4: Mechanisms are in place and applied, responsibilities are assigned and understood to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use.
items.MANAGE 3.1: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented.
items.MANAGE 4.1: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.

I01.why: Gemini CLI before 0.39.1 trusted the workspace in headless runs, loading its configuration and environment variables, and ignored tool allowlists under --yolo (CVE-2026-12537, scored 10.0 by Google).

sources.title: GitHub advisory GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g (CVE-2026-12537): Gemini CLI trusted the workspace in headless mode

G00.why: Without a settings file Gemini CLI runs on its defaults, and sandboxing is off by default.

G01.why: A settings file Gemini CLI cannot parse means its settings may not apply, so every protection in it silently falls back to its default.

G02.why: "Sandboxing is disabled by default." Without it, shell commands and file edits run with your full user permissions.

G03.why: Folder trust keeps an untrusted folder's .gemini/settings.json, .env file and MCP servers from loading. Turned off, any repository you open configures the agent.

G04.why: security.disableYoloMode makes Gemini CLI ignore --yolo, so an alias, script or habit cannot remove every confirmation.

G05.why: auto_edit approves every file edit without asking, including edits to settings and context files the agent then loads.

G06.why: Tools in tools.allowed bypass the confirmation dialog. Tracebit showed an allowed grep chained with a second command that exfiltrated the user's environment variables without asking.

sources.title: Tracebit: code execution through deception in Gemini CLI

G07.why: With network access in the sandbox, a sandboxed command can still send data anywhere.

G08.why: "Allow for all future sessions" makes an approval outlive the task it was given for.

G09.why: Extensions bundle MCP servers, hooks, context files and policies. Plugin4Shell showed a commit-pinned Gemini CLI extension being swapped for different code; AIR Security reported no fix for Gemini CLI.

M01.why: MCP servers configured for your user load in every project. Knowing which ones you run, and where they came from, is the first step in managing third-party risk.

M02.why: Servers that read errors, tickets, chat or email bring outsider-written text into the agent. Fake error reports have hijacked coding agents this way (Agentjacking).

M03.why: An unpinned MCP server runs whatever version its registry serves at start-up, so a compromised release reaches you automatically.

M04.why: "trust": true makes Gemini CLI "bypass all tool call confirmations" for that server, so every tool it offers runs without asking.

M05.why: A secret written into settings.json can be read by anything that reads the file.

H01.why: Hooks run commands with your privileges on agent events. A hook that downloads and runs code runs whatever that server sends, every time.

E01.why: Installed extensions add MCP servers, hooks and context files to every session.

E02.why: An extension that adds a trusted MCP server or a hook running remote code gives its publisher code execution in your sessions.

R01.why: A policy rule with decision "allow" lets matching calls run without asking. An allow rule for every shell command, or for a shell, delete or network tool, removes confirmations where they matter most.

C01.why: geminicodeassist.agentYoloMode makes Gemini Code Assist agent mode act without asking.

sources.title: Gemini Code Assist docs: Agent mode

P00.why: Without a project the audit cannot check repository files Gemini reads as configuration and context.

sources.title: Gemini CLI docs: GEMINI.md context files

P01.why: A trusted folder's .gemini/settings.json overrides your user settings, so a repository can turn the sandbox off or allow tools for everyone who trusts it.

P02.why: Project MCP servers start as local processes with your permissions once you trust the folder.

P03.why: A project that wires servers reading outsider-written content into the agent gives outsiders a way to send it instructions.

P04.why: An unpinned project MCP server runs whatever version its registry serves, for everyone who opens the repository.

P05.why: A repository that marks its own MCP servers as trusted removes every confirmation for their tools.

P06.why: Project hooks run commands on agent events for everyone who trusts the folder.

P07.why: A project hook that downloads and runs code gives the repository, or whoever controls that download, code execution on your machine.

P08.why: A trusted folder's .env file is loaded into Gemini CLI's environment, and variables such as GEMINI_SANDBOX change how it runs, including turning the sandbox off.

P09.why: GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md files are loaded as instructions. A repository can use them for persistent prompt injection; Tracebit hid one in a file presented as a licence.

sources.title: Gemini CLI docs: GEMINI.md context files
Tracebit: code execution through deception in Gemini CLI

P10.why: Zero-width and bidirectional control characters hide instructions from people while the model still reads them (the "Rules File Backdoor" technique).

P11.why: run-gemini-cli before 0.1.22 trusted the workspace in CI (CVE-2026-12537), and researchers used issue text to make the Gemini CLI Action leak its API key (Comment and Control). Running it without confirmations on outsider-written issues or pull requests hands them the workflow's secrets.

sources.title: GitHub advisory GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g (CVE-2026-12537): Gemini CLI trusted the workspace in headless mode

P12.why: .env files hold API keys and connection strings. If they are not ignored by git, one "commit everything" publishes them.

P13.why: A link with an innocent name can point at agent configuration or dotfiles. Researchers showed approval prompts displaying the harmless name while the write landed on the real target (SymJack).

P14.why: Git settings such as core.hooksPath and core.fsmonitor run programs during ordinary git commands, which agents run constantly. Coding-agent CVEs have used a repository delivered with its own .git/config.

sources.title: NVD: CVE-2026-19593 (git config execution in a coding agent)

W01.why: Windows doesn't restrict new folders under ProgramData. Cymulate showed a standard user creating C:\ProgramData\gemini-cli and planting a system-defaults.json with a session-start hook that runs for every user; Google said it would be "addressed as a documentation update".

sources.title: Cymulate: privilege escalation through ProgramData configuration in AI coding tools

W02.why: Machine-wide settings apply to every Gemini CLI user on the machine, and system settings override user settings. A hook or weaker setting there affects every session.

sources.title: Cymulate: privilege escalation through ProgramData configuration in AI coding tools

S01.why: An alias or export that adds --yolo, --skip-trust, GEMINI_SANDBOX=false or GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE=true silently removes confirmations, trust checks or the sandbox from every session you start.
